'''''Lunularia''''' is a [[genus]] of [[Marchantiophyta|liverworts]] whose only species is '''''Lunularia cruciata''''', the '''crescent-cup liverwort'''.<ref name="Edwards-2012">{{cite book |last=Edwards |first=Sean R. |title=English Names for British Bryophytes |date=2012 |publisher=British Bryological Society |isbn=978-0-9561310-2-7 |edition=4 |series=British Bryological Society Special Volume |volume=5 |location=Wootton, Northampton |issn=0268-8034}}</ref> ''Lunularia'' is either the only genus in the [[Order (biology)|order]] '''Lunulariales''',<ref>{{cite journal |author=Söderström |display-authors=etal |year=2016 |title=World checklist of hornworts and liverworts |journal=PhytoKeys |issue=59 |pages=1–826 |doi=10.3897/phytokeys.59.6261 |pmc=4758082 |pmid=26929706 |doi-access=free }}</ref> or may be placed in the order [[Marchantiales]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Flores |first1=Jorge R. |last2=Catalano |first2=Santiago A. |last3=Muñoz |first3=Jesus |last4=Suárez |first4=Guillermo M. |date=2018 |title=Combined phylogenetic analysis of the subclass Marchantiidae (Marchantiophyta): towards a robustly diagnosed classification |s2cid=225165843|url-access=subscription |hdl=11336/142087 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cole |first1=Theodor C. == Description ==
''Lunularia cruciata'' grows large, dichotomously branched green [[Thallus|thalli]] with crescent shaped gemma cups containing disc-like [[Gemma (botany)|gemmae]].<ref name="naturespot" /> This is a unique morphological characteristic not possessed by other thalloid liverworts. Its thallus surface is shiny, faintly lined, and is dotted with tiny air pores. When dried the thallus turns yellowish in color and its margin rolls inward.<ref name="naturespot" />
[[File:Lunularia cruciata archegonial head with sporophytes from Haeckel Hepaticae.jpg|thumb|Lunularia can also reproduce sexually, as illustrated by [[Haeckel]] in this drawing of an [[archegonia]]l head with ([[diploid]]) [[sporophyte]] plantlets. The main plant body ([[thallus]]) is [[haploid]]]]
As in other liverworts, the main plant body or [[thallus]] is a [[haploid]] [[gametophyte]]. The [[Antheridium|antheridia]] of ''L. cruciata'' develops in early spring, the [[Archegonium|archegonia]] develops in spring and sporophytes develop in late summer.<ref name="Kirschner-2010" /> However, records of sporophyte developments and sexual reproduction are rare and scattered. This was suspected to have been the result of the anthropogenic spreading of this species, causing a disjunctive distribution of antheridia and archegonia.<ref name="Kirschner-2010" /> When reproducing sexually, the four archegonia is arranged in a cross-shaped head (hence the specific name ''cruciata'') bearing [[diploid]] sporophyte plantlets. When reproducing asexually, the disc-shaped gemmae are readily dislodged from the cups by splashes of rainwater. They can then quickly "take root" and start to grow in suitably damp places, which is why they are so successful in greenhouses.

== Distribution ==
''Lunularia cruciata'' is distributed across the world, found in continents including [[Europe]], [[Australasia]], [[Asia]], the [[Americas]], and [[Africa]]. It occurs commonly in western Europe, and is native to the [[Mediterranean]] region, where the morphological forms from sexual reproduction are more frequently found there.<ref name="Kirschner-2010">{{Cite journal |last=Kirschner R., Nebel M. & Butterfass T. |date=2010 |title=Observations on fertile populations of Lunularia cruciata (L.) Dumort. ex Lindb. (Marchantiopsida: Lunulariaceae) in Germany |url=https://www.zobodat.at/pdf/Stuttgarter-Beitraege-Naturkunde_NS_3_A_0363-0371.pdf |journal=Stuttgarter Beiträge Naturkunde Serie A [Biologie] |volume=NS_3_A |pages=363–371}}</ref> It is also common in [[California]], where it now grows "wild", and is known as an introduced weed in gardens and greenhouses in [[Australia]].<ref name="Schuster-1992">Schuster, Rudolf M. ''The Hepaticae and Anthocerotae of North America'', volume VI, pages 80-91. (Chicago: Field Museum of Natural History, 1992). {{ISBN|0-914868-21-7}}.</ref> [[Ella Orr Campbell]] believed that ''L. cruciata'' was introduced into [[New Zealand]] sometime after 1867.<ref name="Campbell-1965">{{cite journal |last1=Campbell |first1=Ella O. |date=1965 |title=Lunularia in New Zealand |url=http://nzetc.victoria.ac.nz/tm/scholarly/tei-Bio13Tuat01-t1-body-d4.html |journal=Tuatara |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=31–41 |access-date=27 May 2016}}</ref> The [[sporophyte]]s of ''L. cruciata'' are rare, but has been found in European regions, as well as in [[South Africa]], [[Argentina]], California, [[India]], [[Japan]] and New Zealand.<ref name="Kirschner-2010" />

== Habitat and ecology ==
''Lunularia cruciata'' grows in damp, shaded and disturbed habitats such as path and wall edges.<ref name="naturespot">{{Cite web |title=Crescent-cup Liverwort {{!}} NatureSpot |url=https://www.naturespot.org.uk/species/crescent-cup-liverwort |access-date=2022-04-05 |website=www.naturespot.org.uk}}</ref> It can act as a nutrient indicator because it often grows in alkaline and eutrophic to highly eutrophic soil.<ref name="Kirschner-2010" /> Other habitats include [[loam]], boulders, concrete, exposed tree roots, soil covered logs and in the gaps between sidewalk stones.<ref name="Kirschner-2010" /> ''L. cruciata'' also grows as a horticultural weed in gardens, greenhouses and parks.<ref name="Kirschner-2010" /><ref name="naturespot" /> ''L. cruciata'' is sensitive to frost, and is often found near water, where its gemmae are washed ashore.<ref name="Kirschner-2010" />

== Chemical properties ==
Like many other liverwort species, ''L. cruciata'' produces a dihydrostilbenoid growth hormone, [[lunularic acid]], that is reported to be a growth inhibitor of liverworts.<ref>Lunularic acid, a common endogenous growth inhibitor of liverworts. R. J. Pryce, Planta, 1971, Volume 97, Number 4, pages 354-357, {{doi|10.1007/BF00390214}}</ref> [[Cadmium]] in this liverwort also inhibits gemma germination and apical thallus growth, as well as altering cell and [[chloroplast]] structure.<ref name="Carginale-2004">{{Cite journal |last1=Carginale |first1=V. |last2=Sorbo |first2=S. |last3=Capasso |first3=C. |last4=Trinchella |first4=F. |last5=Cafiero |first5=G. |last6=Basile |first6=A. |date=2004-03-01 |title=Accumulation, localisation, and toxic effects of cadmium in the liverwort Lunularia cruciata |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s00709-003-0028-0 |journal=Protoplasma |volume=223 |issue=1 |pages=53–61 |doi=10.1007/s00709-003-0028-0 |pmid=15004743 |s2cid=25486711 |issn=0033-183X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> [[Acetone]] extracts from ''L. cruciata'' were tested and showed antibacterial properties, but had no effects against fungal activity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Basile |first1=Adriana |last2=Giordano |first2=Simonetta |last3=Sorbo |first3=Sergio |last4=Vuotto |first4=Maria Luisa |last5=Ielpo |first5=Maria Teresa Lucia |last6=Castaldo Cobianchi |first6=Rosa |date=January 1998 |title=Antibiotic Effects of Lunularia cruciata (Bryophyta) Extract |journal=Pharmaceutical Biology |language=en |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=25–28 |doi=10.1076/phbi.36.1.25.4612 |issn=1388-0209|doi-access=free }}</ref>
